title: The Hellenistic Age
subtitle: 323–30 BC · The Successors, the Five-Power System, Greek Cities from the Nile to the Oxus, and the Roman Absorption

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Diadochi and the five dynastic states: Ptolemies, Seleucids, Antigonids, Attalids and the kings of the East, down to Cleopatra

entries.label: The partition of Babylon and the Diadochi
entries.hint: After Alexander's death in June 323 BC the generals at Babylon made Perdiccas regent for Alexander's half-brother Philip Arrhidaeus and the unborn Alexander IV, and shared the satrapies among themselves: Ptolemy took Egypt, Antipater held Macedon and Greece, Lysimachus Thrace and Antigonus Phrygia. The settlement was remade at Triparadisus in 321, where Seleucus received Babylonia, and within a generation the heirs were dead and the generals were kings.
entries.note: Diodorus 18.2–3, 18.39; Arrian, Events after Alexander; Waldemar Heckel, The Marshals of Alexander's Empire (1992).

entries.label: Ptolemy I Soter
entries.hint: Ptolemy son of Lagos took Egypt as satrap, seized Alexander's body in 321 on its way to Macedon and buried it at Memphis and then Alexandria, and took the royal title in 305–304 BC; he was called Soter, saviour, after he helped Rhodes against Demetrius. He founded the dynasty that held Egypt for almost three centuries, the Museum and the royal cult of Serapis.
entries.note: Diodorus 18.28, 20.53; Pausanias 1.6–8; Günther Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (2001).

entries.label: Ptolemy II Philadelphus and Arsinoe II
entries.hint: Ptolemy II, co-regent from 285 and sole king from 283, married his full sister Arsinoe II about 275, a union condemned by some Greek writers but taken into royal cult as the Theoi Adelphoi; his reign was the high point of the Ptolemaic navy and of the Alexandrian court, and the kingdom controlled Cyprus, the Aegean islands and parts of Syria and Asia Minor.
entries.note: Theocritus, Idyll 17; Hölbl 2001; Dorothy Thompson, Memphis under the Ptolemies (1988).

entries.label: Seleucus I Nicator
entries.hint: Seleucus, who had fled Babylon in 316, returned in 312 with a small force from Ptolemy, a year taken as the start of the Seleucid era; he took the eastern satrapies, made a treaty with Chandragupta in about 303 and with Lysimachus and Ptolemy defeated Antigonus at Ipsus in 301, gaining Syria. He founded Seleucia on the Tigris, Antioch on the Orontes in 300 and Apamea, and was murdered in 281 by Ptolemy Ceraunus soon after he had beaten Lysimachus.
entries.note: Appian, Syrian Wars 52–63; Strabo 16.2.4; John Ma, Antiochus III and the Cities of Western Asia Minor (1999); Sherwin-White and Kuhrt, From Samarkand to Sardis (1993).

entries.label: Antiochus III the Great
entries.hint: Antiochus III put down the revolt of Molon and Achaeus, led an anabasis through Armenia, Parthia, Bactria and the Indus country in 212–205 and restored Seleucid claims in the East, took Coele-Syria from Ptolemy V at Panion in 200 and crossed into Europe; Rome's defeat of him at Magnesia in 190 ended the Seleucid hold on Asia Minor, and he was killed in 187 plundering a temple in Elymais.
entries.note: Polybius 5, 10–11, 15–16; Livy 33–38; Ma 1999; Sherwin-White and Kuhrt 1993.

entries.label: Antigonus the One-Eyed and Demetrius Poliorcetes
entries.hint: After Demetrius' victory over Ptolemy's fleet off Salamis in Cyprus in 306 BC Antigonus and Demetrius took the royal title, which Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander took in the following two years. Antigonus aimed at all of Alexander's empire, and at Ipsus in 301 he died in the battle and Demetrius fled with his remnant.
entries.note: Plutarch, Demetrius 17–18; Diodorus 20.53; Richard Billows, Antigonos the One-Eyed (1990).

entries.label: The Attalids of Pergamon
entries.hint: Philetaerus, a eunuch officer of Lysimachus who kept the fortress and treasure at Pergamon in 281, was succeeded by his nephews; Attalus I took the royal title after defeating the Galatians about 238 BC, and Eumenes II and Attalus II, allies of Rome, ruled a kingdom enlarged in 188 and a city of great buildings. Attalus III bequeathed the kingdom to Rome in 133, and it became the province of Asia.
entries.note: Strabo 13.4; Polybius 21–32; Elizabeth Kosmetatou, in A Companion to the Hellenistic World (2003); OGIS 338.

entries.label: The Antigonid kingdom of Macedon
entries.hint: After the Gauls had overrun Macedon in 280–279, Antigonus Gonatas, son of Demetrius, won the throne at Lysimachia in 277/276 and founded a dynasty that ruled until Perseus was defeated at Pydna; the dynasty held Macedon and by its garrisons at the Fetters of Greece, Demetrias, Chalcis and Corinth, a large part of the Greek mainland. Philip V and Perseus fought the Roman republic in three wars.
entries.note: Polybius 2–5, 18; Livy 31–45; Eugene Borza, In the Shadow of Olympus (1990).

entries.label: The Greco-Bactrian kingdom
entries.hint: The satrap Diodotus broke away from Seleucid rule about 250–245 BC and his house was replaced by Euthydemus, who beat Antiochus III's attack and made terms in about 206 BC; his son Demetrius and the later kings of the Euthydemid and Eucratid houses crossed the Hindu Kush and founded the Indo-Greek kingdoms. Nomad invaders ended the Greek cities of Bactria about 145–130 BC.
entries.note: Polybius 10.49; Strabo 11.11; Frank Holt, Thundering Zeus (1999); Rachel Mairs, The Hellenistic Far East (2014).

entries.label: Arsaces and the rise of Parthia
entries.hint: Arsaces, chief of the Parni nomads and later governor, founded the Arsacid state in the Seleucid satrapy of Parthia about 247 BC, whose era was counted from that year. Mithridates I (c. 171–138) took Media, Persia, Elymais and in 141 Babylonia and Seleucia, and then captured the Seleucid Demetrius II, making Parthia a power from the Euphrates to Bactria.
entries.note: Justin 41; Strabo 11.9; Parthian Nisa ostraca; Marek Olbrycht, Parthia and the Arsacids (2021).

entries.label: Mithridates VI Eupator
entries.hint: Mithridates VI of Pontus, who claimed descent from both the Achaemenid and the Seleucid houses, built a kingdom round the Black Sea and in 88 BC overran Roman Asia, where tens of thousands of Romans and Italians were killed in a single day. After three wars with Rome he was beaten by Pompey and in 63 had himself killed by a bodyguard.
entries.note: Appian, Mithridatic Wars; Plutarch, Sulla, Pompey; Adrienne Mayor, The Poison King (2010).

entries.label: Cleopatra VII
entries.hint: Cleopatra, the first of her house to learn Egyptian, ruled with her brothers and son, allied herself with Caesar and then with Antony, and was defeated with him at Actium on 2 September 31 BC; on 1 August 30 Octavian entered Alexandria and she took her life about 12 August. The Ptolemaic kingdom became a Roman province and the Hellenistic state system came to an end.
entries.note: Plutarch, Antony; Cassius Dio 50–51; Dorothy Thompson, in The Cambridge Ancient History vol. 9 (1994).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The wars of the Successors, Ipsus, the Gauls, the six Syrian wars, Raphia, Magnesia, Pydna, the Maccabees, Mithridates and Actium

entries.label: The wars of the Diadochi
entries.loc: Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor and Macedon
entries.hint: Perdiccas was killed by his own officers in an attack on Egypt in 320, after which Antigonus, Cassander, Lysimachus, Seleucus and Ptolemy fought for forty years, with Eumenes' defeat in Iran, the extinction of the Argead family, the claim of the Successors to be kings in 306–304 and the battles of Ipsus, Corupedium and the death of Seleucus in 281. The kingdoms that emerged were the Ptolemaic, Seleucid, Antigonid and the Thracian remnant.
entries.note: Diodorus 18–21; Plutarch, Eumenes, Demetrius; Justin 13–17; Heckel 1992.

entries.label: The battle of Ipsus
entries.hint: In Phrygia the coalition of Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander's force faced Antigonus, eighty-one, and Demetrius; Demetrius' cavalry charged the horse of Seleucus' son Antiochus, pursued too far and was cut off by Seleucus' 480 elephants, and Antigonus died in the fight. The victors divided Asia, and the idea of reuniting Alexander's empire ended.
entries.note: Plutarch, Demetrius 28–29; Diodorus 21 fragments; Billows 1990.

entries.label: The Gauls in Greece and Asia
entries.hint: Celtic war bands under Brennus and others killed the Macedonian king Ptolemy Ceraunus in 279, attacked Delphi where, by Greek accounts, the Aetolians and the god drove them back, and bands crossed into Asia Minor in 278–277 and founded the Galatian settlement in central Anatolia. Antiochus I defeated them in the Elephant Victory of about 275–273.
entries.note: Pausanias 10.19–23; Justin 24–25; Stephen Mitchell, Anatolia (1993).

entries.label: The six Syrian Wars
entries.hint: Six wars between Ptolemies and Seleucids over Coele-Syria and the Aegean were fought between 274 and 168 BC; the First (274–271) and Second (260–253) wars, the Third or Laodicean war (246–241) in which Ptolemy III, according to the Adulis inscription and the Gurob papyrus, advanced deep into Mesopotamia, the Fourth (219–217), the Fifth (202–195) and the Sixth (170–168) ended with Antiochus IV's expulsion from Egypt. Palestine passed from the Ptolemies to the Seleucids in the Fifth.
entries.note: Polybius 5, 15, 28–29; Appian, Syrian Wars; Adulis inscription (OGIS 54); Gurob papyrus (P. Gurob 1); Hölbl 2001.

entries.label: The battle of Raphia
entries.hint: Ptolemy IV and Arsinoe III defeated Antiochus III at Raphia on the Gaza coast with about 70,000 foot including 20,000 native Egyptian phalangites, the first use of Egyptians in such numbers; the victory was won with a larger army than the Seleucid one and was followed by a native revolt in the Thebaid, the beginning of the Great Revolt of 206–186.
entries.note: Polybius 5.79–86; Raphia decree (P. Eleph. and the Raphia stele); Hölbl 2001.

entries.label: The Great Revolt of the Thebaid
entries.hint: After Raphia a native pharaoh Horwennefer, and then Ankhwennefer, ruled Upper Egypt from Thebes for twenty years against the Ptolemies; the royal army reconquered it by 186, and the Rosetta decree of 196 and later amnesties show how much the dynasty had to concede to the temples to recover control.
entries.note: Rosetta Stone (OGIS 90); Hölbl 2001; Jean Bingen, Hellenistic Egypt (2007).

entries.label: Magnesia and the Peace of Apamea
entries.hint: After the Romans had crossed to Asia under Lucius Scipio, with Eumenes II of Pergamon and Rhodes, Antiochus III's much larger army was broken at Magnesia in the winter of 190/189 BC, and the peace of Apamea in 188 forced him out of Asia west of the Taurus, to pay 15,000 talents and to give up elephants and the fleet. Rome gave the lands to Pergamon and Rhodes and withdrew its troops.
entries.note: Livy 37.37–44, 38.38; Polybius 21.17, 21.42–43; Appian, Syrian Wars 30–39.

entries.label: Pydna and the Day of Eleusis
entries.hint: In June 168 BC Aemilius Paullus destroyed the Macedonian phalanx at Pydna and ended the kingdom of Perseus, and in July the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas, meeting Antiochus IV outside Alexandria, drew a circle round him in the sand and demanded his answer before he stepped out, so ending the Seleucid conquest of Egypt. The two events showed a world in which the kings acted at the Senate's will.
entries.note: Livy 44.40–42, 45.12; Polybius 29.27; Plutarch, Aemilius Paullus.

entries.label: The Maccabean revolt
entries.hint: Antiochus IV's measures of 167 BC, the occupation of the Temple, the ban on Torah observance and a new cult, followed the conflict between Jewish priestly factions and brought the revolt of Mattathias and his sons, which recovered the Temple in December 164 and began the Hasmonean state. The revolt was both a war against a Hellenistic king and a Jewish civil conflict about Hellenisation.
entries.note: 1 and 2 Maccabees; Josephus, Antiquities 12; Erich Gruen, Heritage and Hellenism (1998).

entries.label: The Mithridatic wars
entries.hint: Mithridates VI fought Rome in three wars: in the first he took Asia and Athens' allegiance before Sulla beat him at Chaeronea and Orchomenus in 86 BC; the second was a border war; the third (73–63) ended after Lucullus' and Pompey's victories and made Pontus and Syria Roman. Pompey's settlement of the East in 66–62 ended the Seleucid state.
entries.note: Appian, Mithridatic Wars; Plutarch, Sulla, Lucullus, Pompey; Mayor 2010.

entries.label: Actium and the fall of Alexandria
entries.hint: At Actium on 2 September 31 BC Agrippa's fleet broke Antony's and Cleopatra's, and a year later Octavian landed in Egypt, Antony killed himself and Cleopatra followed him on 12 August 30; Caesarion was killed and Egypt became the emperor's personal possession. The last Hellenistic state was absorbed into the Roman empire.
entries.note: Plutarch, Antony 61–86; Cassius Dio 50–51; Velleius Paterculus 2.85–87.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The settlement of Triparadisus, the Ptolemaic and Seleucid administrations, the Rosetta decree and the Peace of Apamea

entries.label: The spear-won land and the royal land
entries.hint: The kings claimed their kingdoms as spear-won land, taken by conquest and held by the army, so that the land and the peoples were the king's, the king's friends and officers were his administrators and the Greek cities were formally free allies but in practice under garrison and tribute. The idea was set out in the Successors' claims and in the Seleucid letters to the cities.
entries.note: Diodorus 18.39, 18.43; Austin, The Hellenistic World from Alexander to the Roman Conquest (2006); Ma 1999.

entries.label: The Seleucid cities and satrapies
entries.loc: Seleucia on the Tigris and Antioch
entries.hint: The Seleucid court moved between Seleucia on the Tigris, Antioch and Sardis, and the king ruled through satrapies and strategoi and a network of new Greek-style cities and military colonies, called Seleucia, Antioch, Apamea or Laodicea after the dynasty. The Seleucid era, a continuous count of years from 312/311 BC, was used for centuries after the dynasty.
entries.note: Appian, Syrian Wars 57; Strabo 16.2; Sherwin-White and Kuhrt 1993; Getzel Cohen, The Hellenistic Settlements in Syria (2006).

entries.label: The Ptolemaic state
entries.hint: Egypt was run by the king and an Alexandrian court through a Greek-language bureaucracy of strategoi, nomarchs and village scribes, with royal monopolies, tax farmers and military settlers on royal land; the Revenue Laws papyrus of 259 BC shows tax-farming under tight state control, and the Zenon archive from Philadelphia in the Fayum shows an estate manager's daily business.
entries.note: P. Revenue Laws (259 BC); Zenon papyri (P. Cairo Zenon); Hölbl 2001; Thompson 1994.

entries.label: The Greek cities and the kings
entries.hint: Inscriptions from Priene, Miletus, Ilion and elsewhere record how cities negotiated with kings by embassies and honorific decrees, asking for exemption from tribute, freedom and the return of land, and in return awarding crowns and cult; the cities' language of freedom and autonomy was a constant diplomatic currency, while royal letters set out the terms of their gifts.
entries.note: I. Priene; Welles, Royal Correspondence in the Hellenistic Period (1934); Ma 1999.

entries.label: The Rosetta decree
entries.hint: The priests assembled at Memphis in March 196 BC for the coronation of Ptolemy V issued a decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek granting honours and tax relief to the temples and recording the king's amnesty after the revolt; copies stood in each temple. The stone found at Rosetta in 1799 made possible the decipherment of hieroglyphs.
entries.note: OGIS 90; Rosetta Stone, British Museum EA 24; Richard Parkinson, Cracking Codes (1999).

entries.label: The Peace of Apamea
entries.hint: The treaty imposed on Antiochus III after Magnesia required him to leave Asia Minor, to pay an indemnity of 15,000 Euboean talents over twelve years and to hand over elephants, warships and hostages including his son Antiochus; it was the first time Rome fixed the boundaries of an eastern kingdom, and its terms were later cited as a precedent in the dealing with Antiochus IV.
entries.note: Polybius 21.42–43; Livy 38.38; Appian, Syrian Wars 38–39.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Ruler cult, Serapis and Isis, the Babylonian temples, the Septuagint and Ashoka's Greek edicts

entries.label: The ruler cult
entries.hint: The Successors were honoured by the cities as saviours and benefactors and then, in Egypt, by a dynastic cult of Alexander and the Theoi Adelphoi at Alexandria, while Antiochus III set up a state cult of the Seleucid line, with a high priest in each satrapy, about 193 BC. The ruler cult was a civic and a royal language of gratitude rather than a belief that the king was a god in the Greek sense of an immortal.
entries.note: Simon Price, Rituals and Power (1984); Hölbl 2001; Austin 2006.

entries.label: Serapis and Isis
entries.hint: Ptolemy I and his successors promoted Serapis, a god who joined Osiris and Apis with Greek features of Zeus and Hades and whose temple, the Serapeum, rose in Alexandria; Isis spread through Greek ports as a goddess of the sea, of grain and of women, with her shrines at Delos from the late third century BC. The cult became one of the main ones of the Mediterranean in the later centuries.
entries.note: Plutarch, De Iside 28; Tacitus, Histories 4.83–84; Hölbl 2001.

entries.label: The Septuagint
entries.hint: The Jews of Alexandria, a large community of the city, translated the Torah into Greek in the third century BC, a work later told in the Letter of Aristeas as a commission of Ptolemy II, and the other books followed in the next two centuries; the Greek Bible was the scripture of the Greek-speaking Jews and later of the early Christians.
entries.note: Letter of Aristeas; Philo, Life of Moses 2; Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (2012).

entries.label: The Babylonian temples under the Seleucids
entries.hint: The Cylinder of Antiochus I, written in cuneiform, records that the king rebuilt Esagila in Babylon and Ezida in Borsippa in 268 BC; the temples and their astronomers continued the Babylonian Astronomical Diaries until the first century BC, and Berossus, a priest of Bel, wrote a Greek history of Babylon for the king.
entries.note: Antiochus Cylinder (BM 36277); Astronomical Diaries (Sachs and Hunger); Sherwin-White and Kuhrt 1993.

entries.label: Ashoka's Greek edicts
entries.hint: Ashoka's rock edicts at Kandahar and Shar-i-Kuna in Afghanistan were written in Greek and Aramaic for the Greek population of the Mauryan frontier; they speak of piety, self-control and the abandonment of killing, in terms taken from Greek philosophy, and name Antiochus and Ptolemy as rulers to whom his envoys went in the Thirteenth Rock Edict.
entries.note: Kandahar Greek edict (Schlumberger and Benveniste 1964); Rock Edict XIII; Romila Thapar, Ashoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Library of Alexandria, Alexandrian poetry, the Altar of Pergamon, Ai Khanoum and the portrait coin

entries.label: The Library and the Museum of Alexandria
entries.hint: Ptolemy I and II founded the Museum, a royal research community with a library near the palace, said by later writers to have held several hundred thousand scrolls, with scholars paid by the king; its librarians, among them Zenodotus, Callimachus, Eratosthenes and Aristarchus of Samothrace, edited the texts of Homer and made the first catalogue of Greek literature.
entries.note: Strabo 17.1.8; Athenaeus 5.203e; Roger Bagnall, Alexandria: Library of Dreams (2002).

entries.label: The poets of Alexandria
entries.hint: Callimachus wrote the Aetia, hymns and epigrams and the Pinakes, the Library's catalogue; Theocritus, from Syracuse and Cos, the pastoral Idylls and the praise of Ptolemy II; and Apollonius of Rhodes the Argonautica, a learned epic on Jason; their short, refined forms and allusive style set the pattern for Latin poets from Catullus to Virgil.
entries.note: Callimachus, Aetia, Hymns; Theocritus, Idylls; Apollonius, Argonautica; Susan Stephens, Seeing Double (2003).

entries.label: Ai Khanoum
entries.hint: The Greek city on the Oxus in northern Afghanistan, excavated by the French mission under Paul Bernard from 1965 to 1978, had a gymnasium, a theatre of about 5,000 seats, a palace and a shrine of Kineas with the Delphic maxims inscribed on a stele, and was probably Alexandria on the Oxus; it was sacked by nomads about 145 BC.
entries.note: Paul Bernard, Fouilles d'Aï Khanoum (1973–2012); Claude Rapin, Mairs 2014.

entries.label: The Nike of Samothrace and the Aphrodite of Milos
entries.hint: The Nike of Samothrace, probably set up about 190 BC in the sanctuary of the Great Gods to commemorate a naval victory, probably of Rhodes, and the Aphrodite from Melos, found in 1820 and dated about 150–125 BC, show the Hellenistic sculptors' interest in movement, drapery and the spiral composition seen from several sides.
entries.note: Louvre MA 2369 (Nike), MA 399 (Aphrodite); Jerome Pollitt, Art in the Hellenistic Age (1986).

entries.label: The Great Altar of Pergamon
entries.hint: Eumenes II had a great altar of Zeus and Athena built on the acropolis of Pergamon in the years after his victory over the Galatians, with a frieze of the gods' battle with the Giants, one of the most dramatic works of Greek sculpture. The altar was carried in pieces to Berlin by Carl Humann's expedition in 1878–1886.
entries.note: Vitruvius 7 pref.; Pergamon excavation reports (Humann, 1880s); Andrew Stewart, Attalos, Athens, and the Akropolis (1993).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Epicurus and the Stoa, Euclid and Eratosthenes, Aristarchus and Hipparchus, Berossus and Manetho, Polybius

entries.label: Epicurus and Zeno of Citium
entries.hint: Epicurus founded his school, the Garden, in Athens in 306 BC and taught that the gods do not meddle and that pleasure in the sense of tranquillity is the good, and Zeno of Citium, a Phoenician from Cyprus, began to teach in the Painted Stoa about 300, with a doctrine of reason, fate and duty that became the most influential philosophy of the later world.
entries.note: Diogenes Laertius 7, 10; A. A. Long and D. N. Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers (1987).

entries.label: Euclid, Eratosthenes and Aristarchus
entries.hint: Euclid's Elements, written in Alexandria about 300, set mathematics in an axiomatic order; Aristarchus of Samos about 270 argued for a sun-centred arrangement of the planets, and Eratosthenes, the Library's head, estimated the circumference of the earth at about 40,000 kilometres in a calculation based on the shadow at Syene and Alexandria.
entries.note: Euclid, Elements; Archimedes, Sand-Reckoner 1; Cleomedes 1.10; Thomas Heath, Aristarchus of Samos (1913).

entries.label: Berossus, Manetho and the native histories in Greek
entries.hint: Berossus, a priest of Bel at Babylon, wrote the Babyloniaca for Antiochus I, with the flood, the kings of Babylon and Chaldean astronomy, and Manetho, a priest at Heliopolis or Sebennytus, wrote the Aegyptiaca for Ptolemy II, which gave the arrangement of Egypt's kings into thirty dynasties, still the framework of Egyptian chronology.
entries.note: Berossus (Burstein, 1978); Manetho (W. G. Waddell, 1940); Sherwin-White and Kuhrt 1993.

entries.label: Polybius
entries.hint: Polybius, an Achaean statesman taken as a hostage to Rome in 167 BC, wrote his Histories to explain how in fifty-three years from 220 to 168 the whole inhabited world fell under the power of Rome; he is the principal source for the Hellenistic state system, and his analysis of the mixed constitution shaped later political theory.
entries.note: Polybius, Histories 1.1; Frank Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius (1957–1979).

entries.label: Hipparchus and the Babylonian astronomers
entries.hint: Hipparchus of Nicaea, observing at Rhodes, compiled a star catalogue and discovered the precession of the equinoxes, using both Greek geometry and the long Babylonian series of eclipses and observations; Seleucus of Seleucia on the Tigris was said to have defended the sun-centred system, and Babylonian scribes kept the mathematical astronomy of the planetary tables.
entries.note: Ptolemy, Almagest 3, 7; Plutarch, Platonic Questions 8; Otto Neugebauer, A History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy (1975).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Ptolemaic monopolies, Delos and Rhodes, the royal land of the Seleucids and the monsoon route

entries.label: Rhodes and Delos
entries.hint: Rhodes, which survived Demetrius' siege in 305–304 BC and built the Colossus from the siege engines he left, controlled maritime law and trade in the Aegean until Rome made Delos a free port in 166 BC to damage it; Delos then became the principal market of slaves and goods, with Italian traders in large numbers until Mithridates' attack in 88.
entries.note: Diodorus 20.81–100; Strabo 10.5.4, 14.5.2; Polybius 30.31; Gary Reger, Regionalism and Change in the Economy of Independent Delos (1994).

entries.label: Royal land and the Seleucid colonies
entries.hint: The Seleucids kept most land as royal land, worked by native peasants (laoi) and granted to cities, temples and courtiers, and settled Greek and Macedonian soldiers as colonists with plots; the Greek and cuneiform documents from Babylonia and Uruk and the survey evidence from Syria show that the network of colonies changed settlement patterns.
entries.note: Seleucid land grants (Sardis, Mylasa inscriptions); Sherwin-White and Kuhrt 1993; Cohen 2006.

entries.label: The Ptolemaic monopolies
entries.hint: Egypt under the Ptolemies had a closed currency and royal control over oil, papyrus, textiles and banks, with a system of tax-farming and royal granaries that made it a major grain exporter and the richest state of the age; it also depended on the Nile flood, and papyri such as the Revenue Laws show a bureaucratic economy managed in detail.
entries.note: P. Revenue Laws (259 BC); Zenon papyri; Hölbl 2001; Roger Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993).

entries.label: The monsoon route to India
entries.hint: The Ptolemies built ports on the Red Sea such as Berenice, Myos Hormos and Philoteras and hunted elephants through the Troglodyte coast, and Eudoxus of Cyzicus, sent by Ptolemy VIII, is said by Posidonius to have reached India with the help of an Indian pilot and the monsoon about 118 BC; the open sea route replaced much of the coastal route.
entries.note: Strabo 2.3.4–5; Pliny, Natural History 6.101–106; Steven Sidebotham, Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route (2011).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Pharos, Archimedes, the Antikythera mechanism and the planned city

entries.label: The planned city
entries.hint: Hellenistic foundations were set out on grids with colonnaded streets and a central agora, in the line of Hippodamus: Alexandria's plan by Dinocrates, Antioch's gridded plan with a long main street, Priene with its terraced blocks on the slope; the plan became the model for Roman colonies and later towns across the Mediterranean and western Asia.
entries.note: Vitruvius 2.pref; Pausanias; Wolfram Hoepfner and Ernst-Ludwig Schwandner, Haus und Stadt im klassischen Griechenland (1986).

entries.label: Archimedes of Syracuse
entries.hint: Archimedes, who studied in Alexandria, proved the law of the lever and of buoyancy, the area of the circle and the sphere's volume, and designed the screw pump, compound pulleys and the war engines that held the Roman fleet at Syracuse in 213–212; he was killed when the city fell. His method of exhaustion anticipated the integral calculus.
entries.note: Archimedes, On the Sphere and Cylinder, On Floating Bodies, The Method; Plutarch, Marcellus 14–19.

entries.label: The Pharos of Alexandria
entries.hint: The lighthouse on the island of Pharos was built under Ptolemy I and II by the architect Sostratus of Cnidus, a tower of some 100 metres with a fire and a mirror, among the tallest structures of the ancient world, which stood until earthquakes of the fourteenth century; underwater excavations at Qaitbay in the 1990s found blocks of the tower.
entries.note: Strabo 17.1.6; Pliny, Natural History 36.83; Jean-Yves Empereur, Le Phare d'Alexandrie (1998).

entries.label: The Antikythera mechanism
entries.hint: A bronze geared device with some thirty surviving gears, recovered from a wreck off Antikythera in 1901 that sank about 70–60 BC, models the motions of the sun and moon, the eclipse cycles and the dates of the Panhellenic games; it had no known equal in complexity for more than a thousand years, and its maker's workshop is not certain.
entries.note: National Archaeological Museum, Athens X 15087; Freeth et al., Nature (2006, 2021); Antikythera Mechanism Research Project.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The treaty with Chandragupta, the Mediterranean embassies, the Greek East and the entry of Rome

entries.label: Greeks and Macedonians in the East
entries.hint: Tens of thousands of Greeks and Macedonians moved to Egypt, Syria and Iran as soldiers, officials, traders and craftsmen, forming the citizen bodies of the new cities and the military settlers of the Fayum; Greek papyri, ostraca and inscriptions from Egypt to Afghanistan show a Greek-language upper class in a mostly native population.
entries.note: Papyri of the Fayum (P. Tebt., P. Petrie); Mairs 2014; Cohen 2006.

entries.label: Seleucus and Chandragupta
entries.hint: When Seleucus came to the Indus about 305–303 BC he made a treaty with Chandragupta Maurya, by which he gave up the lands of Arachosia, Gedrosia and the Paropamisadae and received 500 war elephants, and a marriage or an alliance; the elephants decided Ipsus, and the ambassador Megasthenes lived at Pataliputra and wrote the Indica.
entries.note: Strabo 15.2.9; Appian, Syrian Wars 55; Justin 15.4; Megasthenes (fragments).

entries.label: The first Roman embassy to Egypt
entries.hint: After Pyrrhus' war, in 273 BC Ptolemy II sent envoys to Rome and Rome returned an embassy to Alexandria, with a treaty of friendship, a first contact between the Roman republic and the eastern kings; in later years the Senate was asked by Rhodes, Pergamon and the Egyptian kings for help, and its envoys were received as arbiters.
entries.note: Livy, Periochae 14; Dionysius of Halicarnassus 20.14; Justin 18.2.

entries.label: The dynastic marriages of the kings
entries.hint: After the Second Syrian War Antiochus II was to marry Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, about 252 BC, with a huge dowry, after repudiating Laodice; Laodice poisoned him and Berenice and her son were killed in 246, which led to the Third Syrian War, called the War of Laodice. The marriages of the dynasties show diplomacy conducted by blood.
entries.note: Appian, Syrian Wars 65; Justin 27.1; Polyaenus 8.50; Hölbl 2001.

entries.label: Rhodes and Pergamon at Rome
entries.hint: In the generation after 200 BC the kings and cities of the East sent embassies to the Senate: Rhodes and Attalus I against Philip V in 201–200, Eumenes II against Antiochus and against Perseus, and the Achaean League after Pydna; Roman policy was to avoid direct rule and to weaken the strongest kings, a method that left a series of dependants.
entries.note: Polybius 16.24–34, 21–30; Livy 31–45; Erich Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Greek diaspora, the Galatians and the rise of Parthia

entries.label: The Galatians in Anatolia
entries.hint: The three Celtic tribes, the Tolistobogii, Trocmi and Tectosages, settled in the highlands round Ancyra after 278 BC, taking tribute from the cities and serving as mercenaries for the kings until Attalus I's victory at the Caicus about 238; they kept their Celtic speech into the fifth century AD, and their land became the Roman province of Galatia.
entries.note: Livy 38.16–27; Strabo 12.5; Mitchell 1993; Jerome, Commentary on Galatians 2.3.

entries.label: The loss of the East and the rise of Parthia
entries.hint: The Seleucid hold on the upper satrapies slipped as Bactria and Parthia became independent in the third century, Elymais and Persis had local rulers, and from 141 BC the Parthians held Mesopotamia; Antiochus VII's attempt at reconquest ended with his death in 129, and the Seleucids were left with Syria and Cilicia until Pompey in 64.
entries.note: Justin 38; Josephus, Antiquities 13; Olbrycht 2021; Sherwin-White and Kuhrt 1993.

entries.label: From a Greek state system to Roman provinces
entries.hint: In the century after Pydna the five-power system of Greek kings was reduced one by one: Macedon became a province in 148 BC, Pergamon was bequeathed in 133, Syria was annexed by Pompey in 64 and Egypt by Octavian in 30; the Parthian state alone survived as a major power outside the Roman world, and the Mediterranean became a Roman sea.
entries.note: Polybius 3.1; Gruen 1984; Cassius Dio 51.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Queens and royal women, slaves at Delos, Greeks and Egyptians in the Fayum and the settlers of the king

entries.label: The queens of the Hellenistic courts
entries.hint: Royal women held real political and religious power: Arsinoe II, who ruled with her brother-husband and was worshipped after her death in 270 BC; Berenice II, who governed Egypt during Ptolemy III's campaign; Laodice, whose rivalry with Berenice led to a war; and Cleopatra I, regent of Egypt for her son. Their cults, coins and letters, with the dowries and tax grants recorded, give a rare view of royal women's authority.
entries.note: Sarah Pomeroy, Women in Hellenistic Egypt (1984); Elizabeth Carney, Women and Monarchy in Macedonia (2000).

entries.label: Egyptians and Greeks in Ptolemaic society
entries.hint: The papyri of the Fayum, preserved in cartonnage and rubbish, show that Greek and Egyptian communities lived apart in law and language yet merged by marriage and by the use of both languages in contracts; native priests kept temples and a native law, while the Greek status gave tax advantages, and many Egyptians took Greek names to improve their standing.
entries.note: Dorothy Thompson, Memphis under the Ptolemies (1988); P. Tebt.; Willy Clarysse and Dorothy Thompson, Counting the People in Hellenistic Egypt (2006).

entries.label: The military settlers
entries.hint: Soldiers of the king, cleruchs, received allotments of royal land in Egypt and in Seleucid Syria, were registered in units of cavalry and infantry and married local women; they formed a large part of the Greek-speaking population of the countryside, and later the allotments were passed to their sons and became private holdings.
entries.note: P. Petrie, P. Tebt., P. Hib.; Hölbl 2001; Cohen 2006.

entries.label: The Jews and the Greek world
entries.hint: Jewish communities in Alexandria, Antioch and the cities of Asia Minor made their way in the Greek cities as soldiers, farmers and traders while keeping the Law, and in Jerusalem the priestly aristocracy and the reformers disagreed on how far to adopt Greek customs; the Hellenistic centuries made the Jewish diaspora a lasting part of the Mediterranean world.
entries.note: Gruen 1998; John Collins, Between Athens and Jerusalem (2000); Josephus, Antiquities 12.

entries.label: The slave market at Delos
entries.hint: After 166 BC the free port of Delos became the centre of the slave trade of the Mediterranean, able, according to Strabo, to receive and send on up to 10,000 slaves in a day; the captives came from piracy and the wars of Rome, and the great slave revolts in Sicily in 135 and 104 followed the growth of the trade.
entries.note: Strabo 14.5.2; Diodorus 34–36; Keith Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989).
